tests_declared: Complete neurological examination with motor/reflex documentation

resident.chief_complaint: Squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling sensations in both upper and lower extremities.
resident.history: The patient is a 49-year-old male. Symptoms started approximately three months prior to the initial visit with a squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling sensations in both upper and lower extremities. He reported no difficulty in walking. He demonstrated Lhermitte's sign when extending the neck abruptly. He denied any sensory and motor change. A diagnosis of ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) of the cervical spine had been made before hospital admission.
resident.physical_exam: The patient denied any sensory and motor change on physical examination. Lhermitte's sign was elicited on abrupt neck extension. Motor power and reflexes are not documented.
key_positive_signs: Lhermitte's sign on abrupt neck extension
resident.past_history: Diagnosis of ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) of the cervical spine was made before hospital admission. No other past medical history is documented.
resident.public_message: This 49-year-old male presented with a squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling in both upper and lower extremities, symptoms beginning about three months before presentation. He had no difficulty walking. The patient denied any sensory and motor change on physical examination; however, Lhermitte's sign was elicited on abrupt neck extension. Imaging showed OPLL from C2 to C5 with atlas hypoplasia, spinal canal stenosis from C1 to C5 with cord compression at the atlas ring and an intramedullary high signal intensity area. Preoperative JOA score was 15 points.

imaging.public_message: I have not seen the films and am reporting only the case record's imaging description: OPLL was described from C2 through C5, with spinal canal stenosis from C1 through C5 and especially marked canal narrowing with cord compression at the atlas ring. An intramedullary high-signal area was reported. The record does not specify compression direction or a graded stenosis severity. These findings correlate well with the reported Lhermitte sign and bilateral sensory symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord, most likely at C1-2 (atlas ring) given the marked canal stenosis and cord compression. Lhermitte sign and bilateral upper and lower extremity tingling with truncal squeezing are consistent with cervical myelopathy involving the dorsal columns and possibly spinothalamic tracts. Motor and reflex findings are not documented, so precise long-tract involvement is inferred.

red_flags.finding: Motor power and reflexes are not documented; sensory examination reportedly normal despite subjective tingling.
red_flags.rationale: This is an examination gap, not evidence of an alternative cause. Lhermitte sign is a positive finding and imaging shows cord compression, so the absence of documented motor/reflex changes does not undermine the myelopathic localization.

red_flags.finding: Marked canal narrowing and cord compression at the atlas ring due to atlas hypoplasia, distinct from the OPLL at C2-C5.
red_flags.rationale: If surgical decompression is planned primarily for OPLL at C2-C5, the upper cervical compression at C1-2 may require additional or different surgical consideration. The cord compression at the atlas ring is part of the same cervical myelopathy but could change the operative approach.

neurology.public_message: Findings localize to the cervical spinal cord, most likely C1-2, with Lhermitte sign and bilateral sensory symptoms. Imaging shows cord compression at the atlas ring and intramedullary signal change, correlating well (high match). Red flags: (1) Motor power and reflexes are not documented—a coexisting limitation, not an alternative cause; (2) Atlas ring compression from hypoplasia may change the surgical plan if decompression targets only OPLL levels. No symptom-imaging mismatch.

anesthesia.public_message: The patient is classified as ASA II. The intraoperative mean arterial pressure target is 85 mmHg. Blood loss risk is assessed as moderate. physiatrist_opening.proposed_duration: 3-6 months of structured conservative management with close neurological monitoring
preconditions_for_failure: Development of new objective motor weakness (MRC grade ≤4/5) or gait instability
Worsening of JOA score by ≥2 points from baseline of 15
Appearance of bladder or bowel dysfunction
Progression of intramedullary T2 hyperintensity or new cord compression on follow-up MRI
Persistent or worsening symptoms despite 6 months of conservative treatment
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge the imaging demonstrates significant stenosis and cord signal change; however, the patient currently presents with mild symptoms (JOA 15, no motor or gait deficits documented, only subjective tingling and Lhermitte sign). A structured 3-6 month trial of conservative management—cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, avoidance of high-risk maneuvers, and close neurological surveillance—is a reasonable first step. Surgical decompression is indicated only if there is objective neurological deterioration (new motor weakness, gait decline, sphincter involvement) or worsening T2 signal on follow-up MRI. The success rate of observation and conservative therapy in mild myelopathy without obvious motor deficit is approximately 40%, and a trial can be undertaken safely with frequent reassessment.

The Director and Deputy Director continue to cite the same cord signal change and Lhermitte sign, both of which I already incorporated into my conservative recommendation. The absence of a documented motor and reflex examination remains a gap, but that gap does not itself prove active progressive myelopathy requiring urgent surgery; it simply means that data are needed. A structured 3-6 month conservative trial with predefined objective failure criteria is still a safe and reasonable first step for a patient with JOA 15 and no documented motor, gait, or sphincter deficits. I hold my position.

vice_opinions.assessment: This patient has cervical compressive myelopathy from OPLL C2-5 and atlas hypoplasia causing C1-5 stenosis with marked cord compression at C1 and intramedullary T2 signal change. Although JOA 15 indicates mild myelopathy, the presence of Lhermitte sign, bilateral sensory symptoms, and cord signal change indicate spinal cord injury with a high risk of progression. Surgical decompression is likely indicated; conservative management could be considered but carries risk of irreversible deterioration. The absence of documented motor and reflex findings is a significant gap that should be corrected before final surgical planning.
proposed_options: Posterior decompression C1-C5: C1 laminectomy (posterior arch resection) and C2-C5 laminoplasty or laminectomy with instrumented fusion, addressing both atlas ring compression and OPLL-related stenosis.
Posterior decompression C2-C5 only, without C1 laminectomy, if atlas ring narrowing is judged not primarily responsible for cord compression on further imaging review.

Conservative management with structured rehabilitation and close neurological surveillance for 3-6 months, proceeding to surgery only if clinical or radiological deterioration occurs (as proposed by physiatry).
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior decompression including C1 laminectomy and C2-5 decompression (laminoplasty or laminectomy with fusion).
disagreement_points: The physiatrist's recommendation for conservative management conflicts with my view that cord signal change and Lhermitte sign warrant early surgical decompression; I would not delay surgery for a 3-6 month trial unless the patient is very reluctant or has significant comorbidity.
The surgical extent must include C1: atlas hypoplasia with cord compression at the atlas ring is a distinct pathology; decompressing only OPLL levels C2-5 would leave a critical stenosis untreated.

The choice between laminoplasty and laminectomy with fusion is unsettled: OPLL is often associated with progressive kyphosis, but laminoplasty preserves motion; we need to discuss based on alignment and instability.
The lack of documented motor and reflex findings is a problem: we cannot fully stage the myelopathy or set a reliable baseline for monitoring without this.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree that surgery should be offered now rather than a conservative trial, given the T2 cord signal?
What is your preference for posterior approach: laminoplasty vs laminectomy with fusion, and should we include C1 in all cases?
Should we obtain a full motor/reflex examination and possibly dynamic imaging before finalizing the operative plan?
vice_opinions.public_message: I recommend surgical decompression rather than conservative management: the cord signal change and Lhermitte sign indicate active myelopathy despite JOA 15. I favor a posterior C1-C5 decompression including C1 laminectomy, with C2-C5 laminoplasty or fusion depending on alignment. We need to resolve the extent of decompression and the role of a short observation period. I'd like your view on these points.

vice_opinions.assessment: I agree that the constellation of OPLL C2–C5, atlas hypoplasia with C1 ring compression, and intramedullary T2 signal indicates cervical myelopathy requiring surgical decompression, and Lhermitte sign supports active cord irritation. However, the documented JOA score of 15 without motor or gait deficits leaves room for the physiatrist's short-observation argument; the indication for immediate surgery versus a 6-week supervised trial remains unresolved until we see the formal motor/reflex exam and dynamic films. I favor proceeding with posterior decompression now because cord signal change at the C1 level carries risk of progressive myelopathy, but I want the observation option explicitly rejected or accepted by this group, not by default.
proposed_options: Posterior C1 laminectomy with C2–C5 laminoplasty if neutral/lordotic and stable on dynamic radiographs
Posterior C1–C5 laminectomy with instrumented fusion if instability or kyphosis on dynamic radiographs
Structured observation for 6 weeks with serial neurological exams and repeat MRI, proceeding to surgery if any motor/gait decline or signal worsening
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior C1 laminectomy with C2–C5 laminoplasty if stable and lordotic; instrumented fusion if instability or kyphosis.
disagreement_points: The physiatrist's position that a 3–6 month conservative trial is safe in JOA 15 without documented motor/gait deficits has not been refuted; T2 signal and Lhermitte sign are markers of cord dysfunction but do not by themselves mandate urgent surgery. The group needs to explicitly decide whether the risk of neurological deterioration while observing outweighs the surgical risk.

Whether C2 laminectomy should be included with C1 laminectomy is unsettled: C2 laminectomy may be needed if the OPLL/stenosis extends to C2, but it also risks C1–C2 instability and may require fusion. The director's plan did not specify C2 handling; I need clarity.

The dynamic flexion/extension radiographs may show instability only at C1–C2 rather than C2–C5. If so, a C1–C2 fusion combined with C3–C5 laminoplasty may be a more targeted option than a C2–C5 fusion; this should be discussed once films are available.
deferred_questions_to_director: If the full motor/reflex exam remains normal and the initial dynamic radiographs are stable, do you still consider surgical decompression mandatory, or would you accept a structured 6-week observation with repeat MRI?
Do you intend to include C2 laminectomy as part of the decompression, or preserve C2 and rely on C1 laminectomy plus C3–C5 laminoplasty?
If instability is present, which levels should be included in the fusion—C1–C2 only, or C2–C5 to match the OPLL?
vice_opinions.public_message: I support the director's decision to obtain additional data before finalizing the approach, and I agree that C1 must be decompressed. I want to keep the contested question of a short observation on the table: if the formal exam is normal and dynamic films are stable, we should explicitly choose between immediate surgery and a 6-week supervised trial rather than assuming surgical indication. I favor proceeding with posterior C1–C5 decompression now, but I need clarity on C2 handling and fusion levels.
